intro: An average is **one number that describes the middle** of a group. It is always **between the smallest and the biggest** number. Three tools do most of the work: **the sum** (how many $\times$ the average), **the balance** (the differences add up to $0$) and, for weights, **the seesaw**.

head: Rule
Example
rows: Symmetric numbers: the average is the middle
Evenly spaced: the middle number, or (first $+$ last) $\div 2$
An even count: halfway between the two middle numbers
Add or remove a number **equal** to the average: no change

blocks.caption: The tall towers give exactly what the short towers get: $\;2+4+1=3+4=7$.

head: They ask
Do
rows: the others as **small** as they can be: $\;6$ different positive integers, average $9$: $\;54-15=39$
the others as **big** as they can be: $\;22$ calls in $5$ days: $\;6$

blocks.text: **positive**, **whole**, **different**: each word changes the answer ($1,1,1,1$ or $1,2,3,4$).

head: Tool
Example
rows: the sum $=$ how many $\times$ the average (treat each value as the average)
**The balance**: the differences from the average add up to $0$
Two numbers: the average is exactly in the middle
A base number: work with the differences
A number joins or leaves: compare it to the average of the group it is in
One value changes: share the change among all
Every value changes the same way: so does the average (same order)

head: Idea
Example
rows: Plug in equal values: every letter $=$ the average
An average equal to a letter: write the sum

blocks.caption: Values above, weights below. Weights $4:1$ $\to$ distances $1:4$: the gap $50$ in $5$ units of $10$. **The heavy side gets the small part**: $80-10=70$.

head: Rule
Example
rows: Each value $\times$ its weight, $\div$ the **sum of the weights**
Groups: the weight is the size (reduce it)
The bigger group pulls: the answer is on its side of the middle
Percent shares: start at the low value, add its share of the gap
Backwards: the distances give the group sizes

items: Do I know how many and the average? Write the sum.
One missing value? Use the balance.
Do the values count the same? If not, it's weighted.
Before or after the new value joined?
The plain middle of two group averages, when the groups are not the same size.
Dividing by how many values instead of the sum of the weights.
Counting after the new value joined, when they ask about before.
Four ones when the numbers must be **different**.
